# 1. Introduction

This project explores how daily screen time and social media platform
are associated with sleep duration, anxiety symptoms and depressive
symptoms. The app is intended for adults.

The main analysis uses `data/alternative_dataset.csv`.
Sleep duration is the primary outcome; GAD-7 and PHQ-9 symptom totals
are secondary outcomes.

The results describe statistical associations, not causal effects.
GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores are not clinical diagnoses.

**Data-source limitation:** the original dataset citation, sampling
method and whether these records are observed or synthetic still need
to be verified. Until then, the results should be treated as a
demonstration of the analysis workflow rather than evidence of
real-world health risks.

## Running the project

Open `pips-project.Rproj` in RStudio and knit this document to HTML.

The main analysis runs automatically and saves tables, figures,
diagnostics and session information in `outputs/`.

The app and supplementary scripts are not run during knitting.

# 2. Data checks and descriptive statistics

The analysis script checks required columns, missing values, repeated
or empty IDs, numeric coding, allowed ranges and categorical variation.
It stops rather than silently deleting or imputing problematic records.

Passing these checks does not establish representativeness,
measurement quality or independence between records.

```{r data-checks}
d <- read_screen_data(data_path)

sample_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure = c(
    "Records",
    "Minimum age",
    "Maximum age",
    "Records younger than 18"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(d),
    min(d$Age),
    max(d$Age),
    sum(d$Age < 18)
  )
)

knitr::kable(sample_summary, caption = "Dataset size and age range")
```

```{r population-note, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (any(d$Age < 18)) {
  cat(
    "**Population warning:** the dataset contains records younger ",
    "than 18. The analysis below retains all validated records, so ",
    "it should not be described as adults-only. An explicit age ",
    "eligibility rule is needed before finalising the adult-facing app.\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat(
    "All recorded ages are at least 18. This supports describing ",
    "the recorded sample as adults, but does not verify the ",
    "dataset's sampling or provenance.\n",
    sep = ""
  )
}
```

```{r descriptive-statistics}
descriptive_vars <- c(
  "Age",
  "Daily_Screen_Time_Hours",
  "Sleep_Duration_Hours",
  "GAD_7_Score",
  "PHQ_9_Score"
)

descriptive_table <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(descriptive_vars, function(v) {
    x <- d[[v]]
    data.frame(
      Variable = v,
      N = length(x),
      Mean = mean(x),
      SD = stats::sd(x),
      Median = stats::median(x),
      Minimum = min(x),
      Maximum = max(x)
    )
  })
)

knitr::kable(
  descriptive_table,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Descriptive statistics for the validated dataset"
)
```

# 3. Main adjusted analysis

We fit separate linear regressions for sleep duration, GAD-7 and
PHQ-9. Each model includes daily screen time, age, gender, late-night
usage, social comparison trigger and activity type.

The screen-time coefficient describes the estimated outcome
difference associated with one additional daily hour, holding the
included covariates constant.

Platform is not included in these adjusted models. Sleep is not
included as a predictor in the symptom models.

Confidence intervals use HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard
errors and an approximate t reference distribution. Holm-adjusted
p-values cover the three screen-time coefficient tests.

The reported 95% confidence intervals are individual intervals,
not simultaneous or multiplicity-adjusted intervals.

```{r analysis, include=FALSE}
# Hide this function's direct printing so results appear only once.
results <- run_analysis(
  data_path = data_path,
  output_dir = "outputs",
  seed = 2026
)
```

## Adjusted screen-time associations

```{r effect-table, echo=FALSE}
eff <- results$screen_effects

effect_table <- data.frame(
  Outcome = unname(outcome_labels[eff$outcome]),
  Estimate = eff$estimate,
  CI_lower = eff$conf_low,
  CI_upper = eff$conf_high,
  Raw_p = eff$p_value,
  Holm_adjusted_p = eff$p_holm
)

knitr::kable(
  effect_table,
  digits = 4,
  caption = paste(
    "Adjusted outcome difference per additional",
    "daily screen-time hour; 95% HC3 confidence intervals"
  )
)
```

```{r effects-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7}
print(results$plots$effects)
```

```{r interpretation, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
for (outcome in names(outcome_labels)) {
  row <- eff[eff$outcome == outcome, , drop = FALSE]

  if (nrow(row) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one screen-time estimate for ", outcome)
  }

  cat(sprintf(
    paste0(
      "- **%s:** one additional daily hour of screen time ",
      "is associated with a signed difference of %.3f outcome ",
      "units (95%% HC3 CI %.3f to %.3f), holding the included ",
      "covariates constant.\n"
    ),
    outcome_labels[[outcome]],
    row$estimate,
    row$conf_low,
    row$conf_high
  ))
}

cat("\n")
```

Negative estimates indicate lower outcome values; positive estimates
indicate higher values.

An interval containing zero does not exclude no linear association
at the corresponding two-sided 5% test level. It does not prove
that the association is absent. Statistical significance does not
establish practical importance or causation.

## Unadjusted sleep pattern

```{r sleep-plot, echo=FALSE}
print(results$plots$sleep)
```

This plot groups daily screen time into one-hour bins. Points show
median sleep duration, bars show the middle 50% of sleep values,
and point size shows the number of records in each bin.

The bars represent variability, not confidence intervals. This
descriptive plot does not adjust for the other predictors.

# 4. Held-out prediction check

The script uses a reproducible random 80/20 train/test split with
seed 2026. Models are fitted on the training data and evaluated on
the held-out test data.

The association estimates above come from models fitted to the full
validated dataset, not just the training subset.

```{r validation-table, echo=FALSE}
v <- results$validation

validation_table <- data.frame(
  Outcome = unname(outcome_labels[v$outcome]),
  Test_N = v$test_n,
  RMSE = v$rmse,
  MAE = v$mae,
  Baseline_RMSE = v$baseline_rmse,
  Improvement_over_baseline = v$test_r_squared
)

knitr::kable(
  validation_table,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Held-out performance of the adjusted models"
)
```

- **RMSE:** root mean squared prediction error; lower is better.
- **MAE:** mean absolute prediction error; lower is better.
- **Baseline RMSE:** error from predicting the training-set outcome
  mean for every test record.
- **Improvement over baseline:** one minus model squared error
  divided by baseline squared error. Positive values indicate
  improvement; negative values indicate worse performance.

The script names the last metric `test_r_squared`. However, its
denominator uses the training-set mean rather than the test-set
mean, so it is not the conventional test-set R-squared.

Prediction errors use the units of each outcome. This is one
internal validation split, not external validation or evidence
of reliable individual health forecasts.

# 5. Model diagnostics and limitations

```{r diagnostics, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
set.seed(2026)

for (outcome in names(results$models)) {
  fit <- results$models[[outcome]]
  ii <- sample.int(
    stats::nobs(fit),
    min(2000L, stats::nobs(fit))
  )

  old_par <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

  tryCatch({
    graphics::plot(
      stats::fitted(fit)[ii],
      stats::residuals(fit)[ii],
      xlab = "Fitted outcome",
      ylab = "Residual",
      main = outcome_labels[[outcome]],
      pch = 16,
      col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#176B87", alpha.f = 0.2)
    )
    graphics::abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
    graphics::lines(
      stats::lowess(stats::fitted(fit), stats::residuals(fit)),
      col = "#B34444",
      lwd = 2
    )

    stats::qqnorm(
      stats::residuals(fit)[ii],
      main = "Residual Q-Q plot",
      pch = 16,
      cex = 0.5
    )
    stats::qqline(
      stats::residuals(fit)[ii],
      col = "#B34444"
    )
  }, finally = graphics::par(old_par))
}
```

Review residual-versus-fitted plots for curvature and uneven spread,
and Q-Q plots for departures from a normal residual distribution.
Diagnostic points may be subsampled, but model estimation uses all
validated records.

Important limitations:

- Reverse direction and unmeasured variables may explain associations.
- Some adjusted variables could be consequences of screen use rather
  than confounders; adjustment does not identify causal effects.
- HC3 standard errors do not correct nonlinearity, dependence between
  records or an incorrectly specified mean model.
- GAD-7 and PHQ-9 are bounded totals; linear predictions can fall
  outside their possible ranges.
- Sampling, measurement and data provenance still need verification.

The random validation split can also fail if a rare categorical
level appears only in the test set. If that happens, review the
category counts and validation strategy rather than silently
dropping records.

# 6. Supplementary platform analysis

The script `src/analyses_alternative_data` fits simpler models with
daily screen time and platform as predictors. It also produces
descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, platform comparisons
and interaction tests.

It retains platform categories with at least 30 records and uses
the most frequent retained category as the reference. Regressions
use outcome-specific complete cases. Platform analyses are skipped
if fewer than two usable categories remain.

These models do not include the additional covariates used in
Section 3, and their standard regression intervals are not HC3
intervals. Their estimates therefore need not match the main analysis.

**Before running this script:** change its data-loading block to
read `data/alternative_dataset.csv`, remove `View(actualdata)`,
and install its dependencies separately.

```{r platform-analysis, eval=FALSE}
# Run manually from the project root after correcting data loading.
source("src/analyses_alternative_data")
```

# 7. Shiny app

The app uses the simpler model specification:

`outcome ~ Daily_Screen_Time_Hours + platform`

It does not use the adjusted models from Section 3.

Selecting several platforms averages their separate predictions.
It does not estimate the combined effect of using several platforms.

**Before launching:** change the app's data-loading block to read
the local dataset and install its dependencies separately.
R 4.0 or later is required because the app uses raw strings.

The app is deliberately not launched during knitting.

```{r app, eval=FALSE}
# Run manually from the project root.
# Source in a separate environment to avoid overwriting report objects.
app_env <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
app <- source("src/alt_data_app_script", local = app_env)$value
shiny::runApp(app)
```

## App interpretation caveats

The current app clips predictions and interval endpoints to the
possible outcome ranges. Clipping does not make these valid
bounded-outcome intervals.

When multiple platforms are selected, the result cards average
prediction-interval endpoints. That average is not a valid 95%
individual prediction interval for combined platform use.
Per-platform intervals should be displayed instead until this
is revised.

Symptom bands applied to predicted means are illustrative, not
personal screening assessments or diagnoses.

# 8. Earlier HBSC exploration and simulation

The project initially explored adolescent HBSC data before moving
to an adult-facing app.

The repository contains `data/hbsc_data.csv` and
`src/run_hbsc_analysis_R.r`. Their analysis interface and results
have not yet been checked for this report, so no HBSC analysis is
executed or interpreted here. Adolescent findings should not
automatically be generalised to adults.

The earlier draft also proposed a simulation check. A verified
simulation workflow has not yet been connected to this report.

Generating simulated data alone does not show that regression
recovers known effects. That requires fitting the intended model
and comparing estimates with the generating values, preferably
across repeated simulations.

# 9. Saved outputs

The main analysis writes the following files to `outputs/`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `all_coefficients.csv` | Adjusted coefficients, HC3 intervals and raw p-values |
| `screen_time_effects.csv` | Screen-time coefficients and Holm-adjusted p-values |
| `held_out_performance.csv` | Train/test prediction metrics |
| `adjusted_effects.png` | Adjusted screen-time association plot |
| `sleep_pattern.png` | Unadjusted binned sleep plot |
| `model_diagnostics.pdf` | Residual and Q-Q plots |
| `session_info.txt` | R version and package information |

These files are regenerated when the report is knitted.

The supplementary platform script writes to the separate directory
`screen_time_analysis_results/`.
